subsystems.name: Photometric data source
subsystems.role: provides the ultra-precise, continuous light curves needed to see a moon or ring signal.
parts: space telescope with stable pointing (e.g. Kepler, TESS)

subsystems.name: Systematics correction
subsystems.role: removes instrumental drift and astrophysical noise that would otherwise mimic a weak signal.
parts: detrending algorithms (e.g. cotrending bases, Gaussian processes)

subsystems.name: Transit modelling
subsystems.role: establishes the planet's baseline transit shape and timing so anomalies can be measured.

subsystems.name: Anomaly search
subsystems.role: looks for timing shifts, depth changes, or out-of-transit dips caused by a moon or ring system.

subsystems.name: Follow-up and false-positive rejection
subsystems.role: checks that a candidate is not caused by a background eclipsing binary, starspot, or instrument glitch.

subsystems.name: Theoretical forward models
subsystems.role: predicts what a real exomoon or ring signal should look like for comparison with data.

buildSteps.title: Choose a high-signal target
buildSteps.detail: Select a transiting planet with deep, frequent transits and low stellar noise, ideally from Kepler or TESS data.

buildSteps.title: Extract a clean light curve
buildSteps.detail: Convert raw spacecraft pixels into a brightness time series, then correct for pointing drift and other systematic effects.

buildSteps.title: Measure precise transit times
buildSteps.detail: Fit each individual transit to get its mid-time, depth, and duration, building a timeline of the planet's passages.

buildSteps.title: Search for timing variations
buildSteps.detail: Look for periodic shifts in transit times that a moon's gravitational tug would impose on the planet.

buildSteps.title: Search for out-of-transit features
buildSteps.detail: Examine the light curve between transits for shallow, repeating dips from a ring system or a moon crossing the star.

buildSteps.title: Fit competing models
buildSteps.detail: Compare planet-only, planet-plus-moon, and planet-plus-ring models using Bayesian evidence to see which is favoured.

buildSteps.title: Rule out false positives
buildSteps.detail: Test alternative explanations such as background eclipsing binaries, starspots, or instrumental artefacts.

buildSteps.title: Seek independent confirmation
buildSteps.detail: Observe the target with other telescopes at predicted times to see if the signal repeats.

buildSteps.title: Publish and await replication
buildSteps.detail: Report the candidate with full data and models; the field requires independent replication before a detection is accepted.

prerequisites.why: Kepler and TESS provide the needed precision for planet transits, but the signal from a small exomoon sits at or below their noise floor.
Kepler gave years of continuous data; TESS has gaps, and many TTV signals need many years to become clear.
the statistical tools exist and are widely used, but they must be applied very carefully to avoid false detections.
Hubble and JWST can confirm candidates, but available time is limited and scheduling is competitive.
PLATO, planned for launch in 2026, will provide long, stable photometry of bright stars, improving the odds.

pathway.milestone: continue searching Kepler and TESS data with improved systematics correction
pathway.unlocks: a larger, cleaner sample of candidate signals and better limits on how common exomoons and rings are.

pathway.milestone: targeted JWST follow-up of the best candidates
pathway.unlocks: independent confirmation or rejection of specific signals at higher precision.

pathway.milestone: PLATO and other long-baseline surveys begin operation
pathway.unlocks: many more bright, quiet stars with years of uninterrupted photometry, where small moons are easier to spot.

pathway.milestone: dedicated exomoon and ring surveys, possibly with future large space telescopes
pathway.unlocks: statistical understanding of how common moons and rings are around exoplanets, and their role in planetary system architecture.
